909:
It started with a tabloid. The Red Revolutionaries, a Red Guard group, put out a paper called Red Guard Combat News and wanted it inserted into Liberation Daily and distributed with it. The newspaper refused. At 1 a.m. on November 30, the Red Revolutionaries brought in students from schools across the city, stormed 274 Hankou Road, and took over the lower floors.

⟦0⟧

The Red Revolutionaries had not told WGHQ in advance. On December 1, the Scarlet Guards brought in more than 10,000 people and surrounded the building, shouting that they wanted to read Liberation Daily, that Liberation Daily was the Party's paper. Inside there were only a few dozen Red Guards. They barricaded the doors and windows. Some were beaten and hurt, some fainted.

On the 2nd, people from the Red Revolutionaries came to WGHQ asking for help. Several people at headquarters were unhappy. They said, something this big, and they didn't even tell us first. ⟦1⟧ You thought for a while and said, their general direction is right, the Red Guards have always helped us, we should help them. On the 3rd, WGHQ sent more than 3,000 people from Huangpu and Changning districts.

When you arrived with your people, Hankou Road was jammed solid. Inside the building were Red Guards and WGHQ people. Outside were the Scarlet Guards, ring after ring, and beyond them the onlookers. Both sides were workers. People cursed each other across the human walls, using nicknames only someone from the same factory would know.

The paper's printers were stuck in the workshop. An old typesetter sat by the type cases holding a single piece of lead type. He never put it down. He said he had set Liberation Daily for seventeen years and never missed a day.

By the third day, people outside started throwing things into the building, and people inside poured water down on them. It was December water. It froze as soon as it landed. An old worker from the Scarlet Guards slipped on the ice and fell. He got up, did not swear, brushed the ice off his padded trousers, and went back to where he had been standing.

⟦2⟧

Disputed When WGHQ got involved. Wikipedia says more than 5,000 WGHQ members were already there when the Red Revolutionaries stormed the paper on November 30. Huang Jinhai says the Red Revolutionaries did not consult WGHQ beforehand. On December 1 the Scarlet Guards brought more than 10,000 people to surround the paper. On the 2nd the Red Revolutionaries came asking for help, and Wang Hongwen, “though unhappy with the Red Revolutionaries' rash action, felt their general direction was still right.” Only on the 3rd did WGHQ send people into the building. On the 5th, Wang Yiping and Song Jiwen signed the three resolutions of the Red Revolutionaries and the four demands of WGHQ. On the 8th WGHQ withdrew, and some people cursed Wang Hongwen for “right-deviationist flight.” Huang Jinhai also says there was no physical fighting between the two sides. See “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 5.

History The Red Revolutionaries demanded that Red Guard Combat News be distributed with Liberation Daily and were refused. Around 1 a.m. on November 30 they stormed the paper at 274 Hankou Road. One account says more than 300 Red Guards and more than 5,000 WGHQ members entered the building. The standoff lasted eight days and nine nights. On instructions from the Central Cultural Revolution Group, the “Three Resolutions” and the “Four Demands” were signed. The paper resumed publication on December 7, and the occupiers left in stages from the 9th. WGHQ sided with the Red Revolutionaries and the Scarlet Guards sided with the paper. This was the first large-scale standoff between the two factions of workers. See Wikipedia, “Liberation Daily Incident”; Sina, “Why Red Guards Besieged Liberation Daily for Nine Days and Nine Nights”; the RFA lecture “Attacking Liberation Daily” (all search summaries).

Fiction The old typesetter, the water freezing to ice, and the old worker who fell are the game's invention. The third option is a seed of the dream in which the two factions reconcile.
923:
Signed and Voided

The first of the Scarlet Guards' Eight Demands was recognition of the Scarlet Guards as a revolutionary mass organization. Cao Diqiu signed. The next day the Municipal Party Secretariat said he had been wrong to sign. Why couldn't the Municipal Party Committee protect the people who were protecting it?

In October 1966 the Central Work Conference labeled the practice of Party committees organizing the masses to protect themselves and suppress rebels a “bourgeois reactionary line.” By December, if the Municipal Party Committee recognized the Scarlet Guards, it would be admitting it was still on that line. After Anting, Zhang Chunqiao had signed the Five Demands of WGHQ on behalf of the Central Cultural Revolution Group, and Mao Zedong had said, “On the Shanghai question, Zhang Chunqiao is right.” By now the Municipal Party Committee no longer had the nerve to back the Scarlet Guards. History

On December 25, Cao Diqiu publicly declared the signature void and said he had signed under duress. Chen Pixian said the Scarlet Guard business was the work of Zhang Qi and Yang Shifa. The committee the Scarlet Guards meant to protect dropped them first. Three days later, 20,000 Scarlet Guards entered the Municipal Party Committee compound on Kangping Road to demand an answer. People who had set out to protect the committee were now besieging it. This was the most awkward part of the Scarlet Guards' position. Researchers have also noted that the Scarlet Guards quickly turned to accusing the committee of capitulating to the rebels. History See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 5; Wikipedia, “Kangping Road Incident”; Meisner, Mao's China and After.

Text of the Eight Demands

1. Hold high the great red banner of Mao Zedong Thought and open fierce fire on the bourgeois reactionary line carried out by the East China Bureau and the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. 2. The “Shanghai Headquarters of the Workers' Scarlet Guards for Defending Mao Zedong Thought” is a revolutionary mass organization. The Municipal Party Committee must provide it with all necessary facilities for grasping revolution, promoting production, and its daily work. 3. The Shanghai Municipal Party Committee must make a thorough public self-criticism before the revolutionary masses of the whole city for the crimes of the bourgeois reactionary line it carried out. 4. Power holders at every level under the Municipal Party Committee who carried out the bourgeois reactionary line must also make public self-criticisms before the revolutionary masses of their units, and must attend on time when notified of Scarlet Guard meetings to hear exposure and criticism. 5. On major questions involving the masses, the Municipal Party Committee must reach agreement through consultation with the revolutionary organizations concerned. Any one-sided, unprincipled signature is invalid. 6. The Municipal Party Committee's notice of November 20, which strictly bans private courts and unauthorized arrests, kidnappings, and beatings, must be firmly enforced. 7. Scarlet Guard members taking part in organizational activities should take up as little production time as possible. Necessary rallies and marches are to be treated as holidays. Wages withheld since November 9 must be paid back in full. 8. Staff approved by the Scarlet Guards are all to be handled as personnel on temporary assignment. History Excerpted from the original document reproduced in Li Xun, “The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), ch. 13. Cao Diqiu wrote on it, “Agreed, on behalf of the Municipal Party Committee, to be issued as a document this afternoon. Today counts as official leave.”

The fifth demand was proposed by Wang Yuxi, a Scarlet Guard leader. He later said it was meant to tie the rebels' hands, so that the Municipal Party Committee could not grant rebel demands on its own. The first demand was added at Cao Diqiu's request. Cao later gave two reasons for signing. First, he feared they would go to Beijing and cut off water, power, and transport. Second, “in accordance with the constitutional principle that the people have freedom of assembly and association, all organizations the masses ask to set up are to be recognized.” A little over a month earlier, Zhang Chunqiao had also cited the Constitution and freedom of association when he signed for WGHQ. History See the same chapter.

When Scarlet Guard headquarters saw Cao Diqiu's statement voiding the signature on December 25, one leader said afterward, “My thinking was in chaos. I lost all confidence. I was like a small child who had lost its mother. I didn't know what to do.” History See the same chapter.

927:
⟦0⟧

On the morning of December 23, Pan Yuefa of Scarlet Guard headquarters ran into a few of you in the canteen of the glass machinery plant and invited WGHQ to their rally that afternoon. You said you had no time. Little Pan said he couldn't go either. Lou Jinbao of No. 31 State Cotton Mill was standing nearby. You said, then you go on behalf of WGHQ.

That afternoon the Scarlet Guards held a rally at People's Square, said to be 300,000 strong. It was called “Open Fierce Fire on the Bourgeois Reactionary Line of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee.” Every speaker attacked the committee and said the committee had deceived them before. Cao Diqiu sat on the platform, a target of Scarlet Guard criticism for the first time. Lou Jinbao was invited onto the rostrum. After the rally, the Scarlet Guards handed Cao Diqiu a sheet of paper with eight demands. The first was to criticize the committee. The second was to recognize the Scarlet Guards as a revolutionary mass organization. Cao held out for more than an hour. People from the crowd rushed the rostrum, windows were smashed, lights were pulled down, and he was crushed so hard he passed out several times. In the early hours of the 24th, he signed.

When the news reached WGHQ, several people in the room pounded the table. A little over a month earlier, Cao Diqiu had called you illegal. Now he had signed his recognition of the other side.

The next morning Chen Pixian, though ill, chaired a meeting of the Municipal Party Secretariat and said Cao Diqiu's signature was an error of political stance. On the afternoon of the third day, WGHQ and seven other rebel organizations held an oath-taking rally at Culture Square. Cao Diqiu was brought onstage. He said into the microphone that the signature was void, that he had signed under duress, and that he had never agreed to points two through six. Chen Pixian said the Scarlet Guard business was the work of Zhang Qi and Yang Shifa, that the signature was Cao Diqiu's personal matter, and that the Secretariat had not approved it.

You sat on the platform. When Cao Diqiu finished that sentence, he folded his notes. His hands were shaking. Someone below shouted, the Scarlet Guards are a royalist organization. The shouting came in waves.

A little over a month earlier, in this same square, you had waited for him to come, and he had not come. Now he had come, and this was what he said.

939: Kangping Road · Municipal Party Secretariat compound
941:
The People in the Compound

Lu Genbao and the people around him in this section are fictional. Their thinking is based on how the sources describe Scarlet Guard members. Protect production, obey the Party committee, believe the Municipal Party Committee is the Party. These ideas often lived in the same person.

The “Three Stops” were the gravest charge against the Scarlet Guards. Huang Jinhai says that at a Scarlet Guard headquarters meeting someone proposed stopping water, power, and transport across the city, and that this was later partly carried out. Li Xun examined documents from the time and the later confessions of Scarlet Guard leaders. Li Xun concludes that headquarters never decided on the Three Stops, and that some grassroots leaders acted on their own amid confusion and anger. What actually halted production was that large numbers of Scarlet Guards left their factories to go north and petition, or to avoid struggle sessions. At No. 17 State Cotton Mill alone, more than 2,900 people left. Zhang Chunqiao later named “plotting the Three Stops” as the reason the Scarlet Guards fell. In the eyes of many city residents, this made the Scarlet Guards the side that “sabotaged production,” when production was what Scarlet Guard members had always valued most. Disputed See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 5; Li Xun, “The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), ch. 13.
942:
Perspective shift. You are now Lu Genbao, 36, a maintenance fitter at a state cotton mill and a member of the Scarlet Guards. Fictional character

On the 23rd you were at People's Square, far at the back. You couldn't see the platform. You only heard the loudspeaker say Mayor Cao had signed. The people around you threw their caps in the air. You didn't. You held your cap tight in your fist until it was damp with sweat.

You had been a Party member for eleven years. Whenever a machine in the workshop broke down, people came to you. You joined the Scarlet Guards because you felt the Party committee was still the Party committee, whatever its mistakes, and the machines could not stop. That day at Anting you sat on the train looking at the people on the tracks, and that was the thought in your head.

On the evening of the 25th, the factory loudspeaker said the signature was void and the Scarlet Guards were a royalist organization. ⟦0⟧ Your wife asked you what royalist meant. You couldn't say.

That night headquarters held an emergency meeting at the Gong Wutai Theater, more than 1,600 people. The notice said to wear extra warm clothes. A train driver jumped onstage and said the drivers, ticket inspectors, and dispatchers on the railway were all Scarlet Guards, the trains were ready, and they were only waiting for the order from headquarters. The hall cheered. Only one leader from Jiangnan Shipyard grabbed the microphone and said they must not go to Beijing. Going would only give others grounds to say they had left their production posts, the 800,000 Scarlet Guards would be crushed for it, and their families would suffer too. He was interrupted several times. You sat in the back row. You wanted to stand up and say he was right. You didn't stand up. Before dawn, 1,300 people walked to the train station.

Someone at the meeting also said, if the Municipal Party Committee won't stand by it, we'll stop Shanghai's water, power, and transport and see if it stands by it then. When you heard that, your palms sweated. You joined the Scarlet Guards so the machines would keep running. Nothing was decided on that at the meeting, but the words got out later and became a charge against the Scarlet Guards. On the 27th, headquarters decided to go to Kangping Road and demand an answer from the Municipal Party Committee. On the afternoon of the 28th you followed the column into the committee compound. About 20,000 people filled the yard, with more outside the gate. You sent representatives into the building. The lights inside stayed on. No one came out. After dark, freezing rain began to fall.

⟦1⟧

Next to you sat Old Shen, a Party branch committee member from your factory, who had joined the Party ten years before you. He said, the Municipal Party Committee was sent by the Party to lead Shanghai. If it falls, who will Shanghai listen to? But we're sitting here today to demand an answer from it. When he finished, he was taken aback himself. Beyond him was a young worker from your workshop, a Youth League member. He said quietly, Master, the branch secretary told me if I stand firm this time, there's a Party membership slot for me next year. Master Gu, the model worker in your workshop, didn't say a word. He took out a small notebook and worked out how much yarn was lost with 20,000 people off work today.

Someone in the yard put up a slogan. We want to rebel too, down with Old Cao. Three months ago you had been on West Yan'an Road defending the Municipal Party Committee. Now you were on Kangping Road calling for the overthrow of its secretary. You looked at the slogan and didn't know whether to tear it down.

In the middle of the night, someone threw a stack of leaflets over the wall. They said, Scarlet Guards, get out of Kangping Road. You picked one up, folded it, and put it in the pocket of your padded jacket. You didn't know why you kept it either.

In the small hours you walked home to look in on your child. He was asleep. You didn't wake him. Your wife told you not to go back. You turned up the collar of your padded jacket, walked back, and sat down against the wall. If they don't give us an answer today, we don't leave.

The night before, you, Pan Guoping, and Huang Jinhai had taken the headquarters car to look at Kangping Road. The road was packed with people. You couldn't tell which side was which. History Li Xun, “The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), ch. 14, reconstructs Wang Hongwen's movements during the Kangping Road Incident from Dai Liqing's recollections, Second Regiment leaflets, and Wang Hongwen's own account. Around 8 p.m. he went to the command post below the Xihu Apartments and told Cao Dehong to hold the Hengshan Road junction. He went back to the factory without entering Kangping Road. Wang Hongwen's own account says, “At first I didn't take it seriously... I don't know the whole course of the Kangping Road Incident.” Geng Jinzhang said, “I did my thing, he did his.”

The “three-point instruction” Xu Jingxian gave before the Special Court was that the Ke family home must not be stormed, power must not fall into the hands of the Scarlet Guards, and Wang Hongwen should be told to send people to fight. During his isolation and investigation, Huang Jinhai found his own work notebook from December 1967. It recorded that the Ke family home must not be stormed, not too many people should be arrested, and the rebels should sit down and talk things over on principle. Huang Jinhai also says that during Kangping Road, WGHQ headquarters sent no one. The forces on the scene were the “Red Guard Army” and the Second Regiment. Wang Hongwen, Pan Guoping, Ding Defa, and he drove over once to look. The car stalled outside the Hengshan Hotel, and Scarlet Guards helped push it to start. One says he missed the meeting on the morning of the 29th and that Geng Jinzhang commanded on the scene. 973:
Why the Scarlet Guards Collapsed So Fast

The Scarlet Guards claimed 800,000 members, more than WGHQ. Yet from Kangping Road to early January, they fell apart in under ten days. Several causes were tangled together.

Their backers fell first. The Scarlet Guards were organized with help from the Municipal Party Committee and the Federation of Trade Unions. Once the committee distanced itself from them, headquarters lost its legitimacy, and the Party committees in each factory were under attack themselves and had no time for them. WGHQ had been built from the bottom up, and having an opponent only pulled it closer together. Interpretation Based on Walder's analysis of how the Scarlet Guards were organized.

The center stood on the other side. On the night of the 28th, Zhang Chunqiao phoned from Beijing, and through his wife Li Wenjing and Xu Jingxian told all rebel organizations “not to let the Scarlet Guards seize the fruits of victory.” A month and a half earlier, when WGHQ was stopped at Anting, the center sent Zhang Chunqiao to sign. This time the Scarlet Guards went north to petition and were stopped at Kunshan, and the center sent no one to sign. History

They lost public support too. From the 30th, the railways stopped, the post and telegraph offices shut, and large numbers of Scarlet Guards left their factories. Zhou Enlai ordered that transport must not be cut, and ordered the arrest of Wang Yuxi, the Scarlet Guard leader who had commandeered trains to send people to Beijing. Huang Jinhai says the Scarlet Guards “completely lost the people's support” and “brought themselves down.” Li Xun holds that headquarters never decided on the Three Stops, yet “even angry words never carried out handed the opponent the most solid reason to destroy them.” Disputed See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 5; Li Xun, “The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), ch. 13.

And there was force. In the early hours of the 30th, rebels charged into Kangping Road from several directions. By 6 a.m. more than 300 Scarlet Guard core members had been seized and 91 were seriously injured and hospitalized. Nearly 20,000 walked out of the compound in single file, and their armbands were piled in six heaps. On the 31st WGHQ issued the Extra-Urgent Order, calling for the heads of Scarlet Guard headquarters and of every district and branch to be arrested. History

Disputed Accounts differ on which cause mattered most. Huang Jinhai stresses the Scarlet Guards' own mistakes. Perry, Li Xun, and Walder put more weight on the stance of Mao Zedong and the Central Cultural Revolution Group. The Special Court verdict calls Kangping Road an armed clash engineered by “Zhang Chunqiao in order to seize the leadership of Shanghai,” and says Wang Hongwen “took part in engineering” it.

Li Xun makes two judgments about Kangping Road. First, both sides showed restraint. The Scarlet Guards were unwilling to shed blood even in the name of revolution, and the victorious rebels did not hound ordinary Scarlet Guards, so Shanghai avoided the drawn-out bloodshed seen elsewhere. Second, Kangping Road set a bad precedent. It was the first time in the country that one faction of mass organizations mobilized people to suppress and ban another, with the approval of those who directed the Cultural Revolution. When WGHQ was founded, it cited the constitutional right of association to claim its own rights. Less than two months later, it would not allow an organization with different views to exist. Interpretation See Li Xun, “The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), ch. 14.

The later numbers. A 1968 report by the Scarlet Guard project group said that of 274 core members at city and district level, 8 were arrested according to law, 80 were seized by the masses and handed to public security, then given education and released, and 96 were subjected to struggle sessions. A 1981 count by the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions found that Wang Yuxi, head of Scarlet Guard headquarters, was sentenced to four years, and 243 main members at city and district level were detained. At No. 17 State Cotton Mill alone, 25 Scarlet Guards were seized and handed to the Public Security Bureau. History See the same chapter.

At 2 a.m., Geng Jinzhang blew his whistle. You stood outside the main gate and watched the people in front surge in with clubs raised. All the lights in the compound went out at once, then came the shouting. Someone in the dark kept calling one name, over and over, until his voice cracked.

You stayed where you were. The people behind you squeezed past you one by one.

Geng Jinzhang heard you out, looked at his watch, and gave you half an hour. You took three men in through a side gate. The people in the yard sat packed against the walls. When they saw your armbands, they all stood up. Someone grabbed a bench.

You said there were more than 10,000 people outside. Leave, go out this gate, no one will stop you. No one moved. After a while one old worker left first, then a few around him. Maybe a few hundred people filed out the side gate. They walked fast, and none of them looked back.

The half hour was up. The whistle blew. You were still standing in the yard.

Disputed Casualties. The figure of “91 seriously injured” comes from Xu Jingxian's testimony before the Special Court. Huang Jinhai says both sides were bare-handed and no blood was shed, only bumps and scrapes, and that the Scarlet Guards had broken into the homes of Zhang Chunqiao and of Ke Qingshi's surviving family. At 2 a.m. on December 30, the Scarlet Guard leader in the railway system told all dispatch office staff to go to Kangping Road. From 5 a.m. no locomotives left the depots and no trains ran. See “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 5.

History Rebels began the assault around 2 a.m. on the 30th. By 6 a.m. more than 300 Scarlet Guard core members had been seized, and 91 seriously injured people were sent to the Huadong, Huashan, Zhongshan, and other hospitals. At 7 a.m. nearly 20,000 Scarlet Guards walked out in single file in six columns, and the armbands they surrendered were piled in six great heaps. On the morning of the 30th Wang Hongwen chaired a meeting that ordered the “smashing of Scarlet Guard liaison stations in every district.” See Wikipedia, “Kangping Road Incident”; first round of fact-checking (search summary).

Fiction Letting people out through the side gate and the padded shoe with the blue patch are the game's invention. There was another such shoe below the platform in Act One.
990:
The Extra-Urgent Order

On December 31, WGHQ printed and issued the “Extra-Urgent Order of the Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters.” It said a small handful at Scarlet Guard headquarters were mounting a “counterrevolutionary counteroffensive” and “preparing to create the Three Stops across the whole city.” It demanded that the heads of Scarlet Guard Shanghai headquarters and of every district and branch all be arrested and delivered to the Public Security Bureau, and that rebel members take over the posts the Scarlet Guards had left. History See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 5; Wikipedia, “Kangping Road Incident.”

Unverifiable The order was issued in the name of WGHQ. None of the material available today records Wang Hongwen signing it by hand. The part of the Special Court verdict on Wang Hongwen says only that he “took part in engineering the Kangping Road armed clash in Shanghai” and does not mention this order. The game has you sign the list so that the document has a specific person putting pen to paper.

According to Wang Weiguo's posthumous manuscript, when WGHQ sent Scarlet Guards to be locked up, Wang Weiguo of the Fourth Air Force Army refused to take them and ordered every sub-bureau not to take them either. Huang Jinhai believes Zhang Chunqiao's words “don't arrest too many people” were aimed at this very order.

A nurse asked which side you were on. You said WGHQ. She ignored you after that. An old worker woke up, saw your armband, and turned his face to the wall. As you left, his wife ran after you and asked whether he would be arrested. You had no answer.

History The fullest quotation of the Extra-Urgent Order is in Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 5. It says a small handful at Scarlet Guard headquarters were “preparing to create the Three Stops (stopping work, water, and power) across the whole city,” and its second item required rebel members to take over the posts the Scarlet Guards had left. History On December 31 WGHQ printed and issued the Extra-Urgent Order, demanding that “the heads of the Workers' Scarlet Guards Shanghai headquarters and of every district and branch all be arrested and delivered to the Public Security Bureau.” See Wikipedia, “January Storm” (search summary).

1007: No. 17 State Cotton Mill · Cotton yarn storeroom
1008:
Master Qian was taken away on January 2. The Public Security Bureau had more people than it could take that day, so he was sent back to the mill and locked in the cotton yarn storeroom behind the spinning workshop.

His guards were a few young workers. One of them was his own apprentice. Every night they held a meeting and told him to confess. He did not know what he was supposed to confess. He said yes, he had spat on October 10, and he admitted he was wrong. They said, that's not what we're asking about.

On the fifth night, someone beat his legs with a carrying pole. The apprentice stood in the doorway. He did not go in, and he did not leave.

On the tenth day he was released, because someone from the Public Security Bureau came and said this man was not on the city's list and no one knew who had added him. He was helped out of the storeroom. His left leg never straightened again.

Later he was moved to watching the factory gate. Every morning at the shift change, he stood at the gate on his crutch, watching people come and go.

In 1977, during the mill's investigation, he came on his crutch to testify. He spoke very evenly. When he finished, he asked if he could have a glass of water.
